summary: Presents the High-level Entity Management Protocol (HEMP), the application protocol used by HEMS to manage network entities such as hosts, gateways and front-end machines. It assumes the reader knows ASN.1 and the system described in RFC 1021.

plainLanguage.summary: HEMP is a protocol for managing network devices from a central place. It gives every message the same shape, adds optional sections for checking who sent a message and for hiding its contents, and defines the message types a manager and a device exchange.

questions: how does hems talk to network devices
subtitle: A 1987 application protocol for managing hosts, gateways and front-end machines over a network.

tldr.problem: Management applications needed one agreed way to talk to the hosts, gateways and front-end machines they controlled, including a way to check who was talking and to hide sensitive monitoring data.
tldr.mechanism: HEMP defines an ASN.1 encoded message with a fixed set of sections: a leader, optional encryption and reply-encryption sections, an optional authentication section, a common header and an application-specific data section.
tldr.outcome: The RFC defines five message types, two authentication types and a table of protocol error codes, and it says to run HEMP over TCP for requests and UDP for events. The RFC Editor index lists its status as unknown, and no later RFC obsoletes it.

today: RFC 1022 is an October 1987 memo describing HEMP as a component of the High-Level Entity Management System, and the RFC Editor index lists its status as unknown. No later RFC obsoletes it, so it is kept here as a record of that management protocol.

sections.title: What HEMP Does
sections.content:
The High-Level Entity Management Protocol (HEMP) provides an encapsulation system and a set of services for communication between applications and managed entities. It is an application protocol that relies on existing transport protocols to deliver HEMP messages to their destinations, and it is a component of the High-Level Entity Management System (HEMS) described in RFC 1021. The protocol is targeted at management interactions between applications and entities, and is believed suitable for both monitoring and control interactions.

The authors state that HEMP provides what they believe are the three essential features of a management protocol: a standard encapsulation scheme for all interactions, an authentication facility that can be used both to verify messages and to limit access to managed systems, and the ability to encrypt messages to protect sensitive information.

A HEMP message is an arbitrarily long sequence of octets. The memo assumes a knowledge of ASN.1, the ISO data encoding standard, whose two parts are International Standard 8824 for the specification and International Standard 8825 for the encoding rules.
sections.plainLanguage: HEMP is the language a manager program uses to talk to a device it looks after. It is an application protocol, so it sits on top of an ordinary transport such as TCP rather than replacing it. It aims to cover both watching a device and commanding it.

sections.title: Requests, Replies and Events
sections.content:
Five types of messages are defined: request, event, reply, and protocol error and application error messages. Reply, protocol error and application error messages are only sent in reaction to a request message, and are referred to collectively as responses.

Two kinds of interaction are envisaged. A message exchange happens between an application and an entity managed by that application: the application sends a request to retrieve information or give instructions, and the entity replies with a response, either a reply message if the request was valid or an error message if it was not, for example because authentication failed. One response per request is expected, though the protocol does not preclude several. The second kind of interaction is unsolicited messages from an entity to the management centres responsible for managing it.

Event messages are unsolicited notices sent by an entity to an address that is expected to correspond to one or more management centres. A single address may correspond to a multicast address and so reach multiple hosts. Events typically alert management centres to important changes in the entity's state, such as an interface going down or the entity running out of network buffers.

Protocol error messages are generated when errors are found while processing the HEMP encapsulation of the message. Errors that occur during the processing of the message contents are application errors. Because the processing agent may have started sending a reply before an error is discovered, an application error may show up inside the reply message instead of in a separate message. Entities are not required to send error messages, because on secure networks that may be undesirable, although on friendly networks their use is encouraged.
sections.plainLanguage: A manager asks a device a question with a request, and the device answers with a reply or an error. A device can also send an event on its own to announce something, such as an interface going down, and one event address can reach several management centres at once. Error messages are optional, because a reply that says nothing may be safer on a secure network.

sections.title: The Shape of a HEMP Message
sections.content:
Every HEMP message has the same general form, shown in Figure 1 of the RFC: a leader, then the encryption section, the reply encryption section, the authentication section, the common header, and the data section. The leader is simply the ASN.1 tag and the message length, and the sections are also encoded in ASN.1, as the following definition shows.

HempMessage ::= [0] IMPLICIT SEQUENCE { [0] IMPLICIT EncryptSection OPTIONAL, [1] IMPLICIT ReplyEncryptSection OPTIONAL, [2] IMPLICIT AuthenticateSection OPTIONAL, [3] IMPLICIT CommonHeader, [4] IMPLICIT Data }

The order of the sections is significant. The encryption section comes first so that all the sections after it, which may contain sensitive information, can be encrypted. The authentication section comes before the header so that a message that fails authentication can be discarded without the header being processed at all.

The common header holds generic information about the message. It contains a link field, which indicates which version of HEMS is in use; a messageType field, whose value is request (0), reply (1), event (2), protocol error (3) or application error (4); a messageId, a unique bit identifier that is set in the request message and echoed in the response so that applications can match a response to its request; and a resourceId, which is defined for ISO compatibility and corresponds to the resource ID used by the Common Management Information Protocol.

The messageId should be chosen so that a substantial period of time elapses before it is reused by a particular application, even across machine crashes. Event messages use the same field to carry the number of the current event, so that comparing the numbers of events that were lost detects gaps. The event messageId should be reset to 0 on every reboot, and by convention the event message with a messageId of 0 is always a reboot event.

The data section contains the message specific data. Its format is ASN.1 ANY, and its contents are application specific and, with the exception of protocol error messages, outside the scope of the memo.
sections.plainLanguage: Every HEMP message is a stack of parts in a fixed order, so a receiver always knows where to look. The parts that need protecting come before the parts that describe the message, which lets a receiver throw a bad message away before it even reads the header.

sections.title: Authenticating and Encrypting Messages
sections.content:
The authentication section contains the data a receiver needs to authenticate the message, and it is a sequence of an authenticateType number and an authenticateData field. If the section is omitted, the message is not authenticated. Two types are defined. The password scheme uses authenticateType 1 with the password as an octet string of any length: the entity checks it against an entity-specific password assigned to that entity, and accepts the request for processing if they match. Authentication by encryption method uses authenticateType 2 with a NULL data field, which says that authentication was implicit in the encryption method; recipients should confirm that the encryption method does indeed provide authentication.

If a message fails authentication it should be discarded. If the authentication type is unknown or the section is omitted, the message may be discarded or processed at the discretion of the implementation, and requests with unknown authentication types are recommended to be logged as potential intrusions but not processed.

The encryption section holds the data needed to decrypt the message, again as a type number and an ANY field. If it is omitted, no decryption is required. If it is present, the type number names the encryption method and the data field holds whatever the receiver must have, for example a key. If the message has been encrypted, data is encrypted starting with the first octet after the encryption section. No encryption types are assigned at the time of writing.

The reply encryption section lets a management agent ask for a response that is encrypted even when the request was not, or encrypted with a different key or a different scheme. It has the same shape, with replyEncryptType and replyEncryptData. If it is omitted, the reply should be encrypted in the manner specified by the encryption section. If it is present, the reply must contain an appropriate encryption section that says the requested method is in use. If the entity does not support the requested reply encryption method, it may send no reply at all, and may at the discretion of the implementor send a protocol error message.

The RFC notes that encryption in HEMP does not protect against traffic analysis, because HEMP interactions are expected to have distinct signatures, and suggests link-level encryption for organizations concerned at that level.
sections.plainLanguage: Two optional parts of a HEMP message protect it. The authentication part says who sent the message, either with a password checked against one held by the device or by pointing to the encryption method that already proves it. The encryption part tells the receiver how to decrypt the rest. A request can also ask for a reply to be encrypted in a particular way.

sections.title: Protocol Error Messages
sections.content:
Protocol error messages are tied closely to the definition of HEMP, so the memo defines the contents of the data section for them. The format was chosen to agree with the error message format and ASN.1 type used for language processing errors in RFC 1024, and the error codes were chosen so that they do not overlap. The data section holds a protoErrorCode, a protoErrorOffset and a protoErrorDescribed string. The offset is the number of the octet in which the error was discovered, with the first octet in the message being octet number 0, and the description gives more detail about the particular error.

The defined codes are 0, reserved and not used; 1, an ASN.1 format error such as an unknown type or a violation of the ASN.1 syntax; 2, a wrong HEMP version number, which the RFC says may be an indication of possible network intrusion and should be logged at sites concerned with security; 3, an authentication error, which is defined for completeness but strongly discouraged in use, because returning authentication failure information may aid intruders in cracking the authentication system, and which is recommended to be logged as a possible security problem; 4, a reply encryption type that is not supported; 5, a failure to decrypt, which means the entity could not read the common header to find the messageId, so the messageId field should be set to 0; and 6, an application failure that made it impossible to process the message.
sections.plainLanguage: When something goes wrong before the request can be understood, the device can answer with a protocol error that names the kind of fault and points at the octet where it was found. The RFC is careful about the authentication error, because telling a stranger that a password failed helps them guess it.

sections.title: Choosing a Transport Protocol
sections.content:
The RFC reports considerable debate about the transport protocol to use under HEMP, part of the problem being that HEMP is used for two different kinds of interaction. Request-response exchanges may involve arbitrary amounts of data in both directions and are believed to require a reliable transport mechanism, while event messages are typically small and need not be reliably delivered.

Public opinion seemed to lean towards running HEMP over a transaction protocol, as discussed generally in RFC 955, but the community was still experimenting with transaction protocols and many groups wanted to implement HEMP now. The memo therefore defines two transport protocols for use with HEMP. Groups that want an implementation in the near future should use a combination of the Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) and the User Datagram Protocol (UDP) under HEMP: TCP for all request-response interactions, and UDP to send event messages. Using UDP to support request-response interactions is strongly discouraged.

More forward-looking groups are encouraged to implement HEMP over a transaction protocol, in particular the Versatile Message Transaction Protocol (VMTP), for which experiments were planned.
sections.plainLanguage: Requests carry a lot of data and need a reliable connection, so they go over TCP. Events are small and need not arrive, so they go over UDP. The RFC also points at transaction protocols as the better long-term choice.
